title: From Blueprint to Production: How Rambus Brings Commercial-Grade Caliptra Security to AI SoCs
gist: Rambus announced a production-ready CryptoManager Root of Trust that wraps around the unmodified open-source Caliptra core, targeting the gap between the open spec and commercially certified AI SoC security. The article presents it as covering physical attack defense, post-quantum cryptographic agility and certification readiness.

insights.claim: Caliptra is an open-source specification meant to standardize the silicon Root of Trust architecture across cloud and data-centre environments, but a large gap remains between the spec and commercially deployable silicon.
insights.speaker: Kalar Rajendiran
insights.so_what: Open standards create room for commercial IP vendors to monetize hardening.

insights.claim: An open Caliptra core lacks platform-wide security orchestration, and moving from a shared GitHub repository to formal cryptographic certifications is resource-intensive, leaving chip vendors with integration and schedule risk.
insights.speaker: Kalar Rajendiran
insights.so_what: Integration and certification friction is the sales argument for commercial RoT IP.
insights.locator: Second, moving from a shared GitHub repository

insights.claim: Rambus introduced the CryptoManager Root of Trust for the Caliptra specification, a production-ready hardware subsystem that acts as security orchestrator around the unmodified Caliptra core rather than replacing it.
insights.speaker: Kalar Rajendiran
insights.so_what: New security IP product in Rambus's line, shown at the AI Infra Summit.
insights.locator: wraps around the unmodified Caliptra core

insights.claim: The Rambus design adds a secure RISC-V processor, protected memory, dedicated cryptographic accelerators and drivers to extend security visibility across the whole SoC, plus architecture layouts and direct vendor support.
insights.speaker: Kalar Rajendiran
insights.so_what: Positioned as a subsystem sale including support, not just a licensed core.

insights.claim: Commercial AI data-centre silicon needs proven side-channel and fault-injection countermeasures and hardware-enforced isolation, which open standards rarely specify.
insights.speaker: Kalar Rajendiran
insights.so_what: Physical attack resistance is a differentiator for security IP.

insights.claim: Because quantum computing threatens modern encryption, commercial roots of trust must blend classical algorithms such as AES, SHA and RSA with post-quantum standards such as ML-KEM and ML-DSA.
insights.speaker: Kalar Rajendiran
insights.so_what: PQC support is becoming table stakes for security IP.

insights.claim: Achieving FIPS 140-3, PSA or SESIP compliance with unassisted open-source blocks introduces large schedule risk, while an implementation packaged with verification test benches and reference designs accelerates time-to-market.
insights.speaker: Kalar Rajendiran
insights.so_what: Certification readiness is a purchase driver for hyperscaler-grade silicon.

insights.claim: Modern data-centre environments are built from a web of custom accelerators, GPUs and distinct processing units rather than uniform processors, which makes securing the underlying silicon foundational.
insights.speaker: Kalar Rajendiran
insights.so_what: Heterogeneous AI infrastructure expands the hardware security attack surface and IP demand.
